title_en: Luo Shikai v. Staples Company and Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office — administrative dispute over invalidation of design patent right
ruling_gist_en: 1. Grounds for patent invalidity can be divided into two types: absolute invalidity grounds and relative invalidity grounds, which differ significantly in the nature of the regulated object, legislative purpose, and other aspects. The invalidity ground concerning a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right is a relative invalidity ground. When the provisions of Article 45 of the Patent Law regarding the scope of the requesting party are applied to the invalidity ground of conflict of rights, based on the essential attributes of relative invalidity grounds, legislative purpose, and the effect on legal order, the standing of the person requesting the invalidation declaration should be limited. In principle, only the holder of the prior legal right and its interested parties may assert such ground.

full_text_en:
Luo Shikai v. Staples Inc. and the Patent Reexamination Board of the National Intellectual Property Administration — Administrative dispute over invalidation of design patent

[Ruling Summary]

I. Grounds for patent invalidation may be categorized into two types: absolute grounds and relative grounds, which differ significantly in the essence of the regulated object, legislative purpose, and other aspects. A ground for invalidation concerning a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right belongs to relative grounds. When the provisions of Article 45 of the Patent Law on the scope of persons who may file a request are applied to the ground of conflict of rights, the standing of the requester for invalidation should be restricted based on factors such as the essential nature of the relative ground, legislative purpose, and effect on legal order. In principle, only the holder of the prior legal right and interested parties may assert such ground.

II. In administrative litigation proceedings, after a people's court accepts a related lawsuit, to ensure the stability of the proceedings and avoid uncertainty in the litigation, the standing of a party is not lost simply because the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit subsequently changes. The administrative procedure for patent invalidation is a quasi-judicial proceeding, and the principle of party constancy may also serve as a reference for such procedure. For a requester who meets the standing requirements at the time of initiating the invalidation administrative procedure, even if the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit subsequently changes, the requester does not automatically lose standing.

Administrative Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2017) Zui Gao Fa Xing Shen No. 8622

Applicant for Retrial (First Instance Third Party, Second Instance Appellant): Staples Inc. Domicile: 500 Staples Drive, Framingham, MA 01702, U.S.A.

Legal Representative: Erich G. Rhynhart, Senior Counsel of the Company.

Agent Ad Litem: Liu Jun, Attorney at Guangdong Jun Zhi Quan Law Firm.

Respondent (First Instance Plaintiff, Second Instance Appellee): Luo Shikai, male, born May 18, 1969, General Manager of Maoxin Hardware Products (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., domiciled in Taipei County, Taiwan Region.

Agent Ad Litem: Zhang Liujian, Attorney at Beijing King & Wood (Shenzhen) Law Firm.

First Instance Defendant: Patent Reexamination Board of the National Intellectual Property Administration. Domicile: Floors 10-12, Yingu Building, No. 9, Beisihuan West Road, Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Ge Shu, Deputy Director of the Board.

Agent Ad Litem: Yang Fengyun, Examiner of the Board.

Agent Ad Litem: Liu Xinlei, Examiner of the Board.

The applicant for retrial, Staples Inc., filed an application for retrial with this Court, dissatisfied with the administrative judgment (2016) Jing Xing Zhong No. 2901 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court in the case of the administrative dispute over the invalidation of a design patent with the respondent, Luo Shikai, and the first instance defendant, the Patent Reexamination Board of the National Intellectual Property Administration (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board). This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law to conduct a review, which has now been concluded.

Staples Inc. applied for retrial on the following grounds: (1) The second instance judgment erred in the application of law. 1. Regarding the standing of a requester in the patent invalidation procedure, none of the previous versions of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China imposed restrictions, all providing that "any entity or individual" may file a request. The second instance court, in its judgment, held that the standing of the requester should be limited to the right holder or interested party, which clearly violates the provisions of the law and constitutes a de facto creation of law, and such major issues of law application should naturally be clarified by the highest judicial authority. 2. The provisions of Article 66 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China as revised in 2010 are requirements for evidence when the Patent Reexamination Board accepts a case, not a limitation on the standing of the requester. The second instance judgment erroneously relied on this provision to hold that the requester should be limited to the right holder or interested party, constituting an error in the application of law. (2) The view of the second instance court in this case contradicts its views in prior judgments, presenting self-contradiction. In prior effective judgments, the second instance court held that Article 45 of the Patent Law as amended in 2000 did not impose any restrictive provisions on the standing of a person filing a request for invalidation, and accordingly overturned the Patent Reexamination Board's decision on the invalidation request based on the grounds that the requester's standing was limited to the right holder or interested party. In this case, the same court made a contrary finding, holding that the requester's standing should be restricted and limited to the right holder or interested party. In the absence of any amendment or adjustment to the law, the second instance court, within less than two years, rendered two effective judgments with completely opposite views, violating its own precedents and causing confusion for the public. (3) Staples Inc. is a specific requester who filed the invalidation request on the ground that the design patent in question conflicts with a prior legal right. The first and second instance judgments erred in fact-finding. Even if the second instance judgment's conclusion that the standing of the requester should be limited to the right holder or interested party is correct, Staples Inc. nevertheless qualifies as a right holder or interested party. 1. Staples Inc. was the copyright holder of the prior work at the time of filing the invalidation request, as clearly found in the Patent Reexamination Board's Invalidation Request Examination Decision No. 20813 (hereinafter referred to as the Decision under Review). Therefore, the issue of the requester's standing should be determined based on the rights status of Staples Inc. at the time of filing the invalidation request. 2. During the examination of the patent invalidation request, Staples Inc. transferred its copyright to another person, but this does not mean that the standing to request invalidation was also transferred. 3. Even if Staples Inc. is not the copyright holder in the strict sense after the transfer of rights, it bears a warranty against defects in the transferred rights and still has an interest relationship with the current copyright holder, thus qualifying as an interested party closely related to the current copyright holder. The first and second instance judgments erred in fact-finding. For the above reasons, Staples Inc. requests this Court to set aside the first and second instance judgments and uphold the Decision under Review of the Patent Reexamination Board.

Luo Shikai submitted comments stating that at the time the Patent Reexamination Board accepted this case, Staples Inc. was a proper requester for invalidation, but during the invalidation administrative procedure, it transferred the copyright in the work in question to a third party. The Patent Reexamination Board, without considering the intent of the new right holder, rendered the Decision under Review solely based on Staples Inc.'s invalidation request, which was erroneous. The second instance court correctly found this. The evidence submitted by Staples Inc. is insufficient to prove that it was the prior copyright holder or an interested party. Luo Shikai requests this Court to dismiss Staples Inc.'s application for retrial.

The Patent Reexamination Board submitted comments stating that based on the evidence submitted by Staples Inc. during the invalidation administrative procedure, it can be lawfully determined that Staples Inc. held a prior legal and valid copyright at the time of filing the invalidation request, and that the design patent in question conflicts with the prior copyright, failing to comply with Article 23 of the Patent Law. The second instance judgment found the facts unclear and erroneously applied laws and regulations. The Patent Reexamination Board requests this Court to set aside the second instance judgment and uphold the Decision under Review.

Upon review, this Court finds that the Patent Law as amended in 2000 is applicable to this case. Based on the applicant's grounds for retrial, the respondent's response, and the facts of the case, the focal issues in the retrial review stage are: the standing of a requester who files an invalidation request on the ground that the design patent conflicts with another person's prior legal right; whether a requester who meets the standing requirements at the time of initiating the invalidation administrative procedure loses standing due to a subsequent change in the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit; and whether the second instance judgment correctly found that Staples Inc. is not the copyright holder of the work in question or an interested party.

(I) The issue of the standing of a requester who files an invalidation request on the ground that the design patent conflicts with another person's prior legal right

Article 45 of the Patent Law provides: "As of the date of announcement of the grant of the patent right by the patent administration department under the State Council, any entity or individual that considers the grant of the patent right not to be in conformity with the relevant provisions of this Law may request the Patent Reexamination Board to declare the patent right invalid." From the literal meaning of this provision, it does not impose any restriction on the scope of persons who may file a request for invalidation. Nevertheless, if the literal meaning of a legal provision is overly broad and, in specific circumstances, its interpretation according to the literal meaning would lead to incompatibility with the essence of the regulated object, legislative purpose, and effect on legal order, resulting in clearly inappropriate legal consequences, a restrictive interpretation of the literal meaning of the legal provision may be justified in specific circumstances, as a matter of legal principle. In this case, the requester for invalidation filed the request on the ground that the design patent granted does not conflict with another person's prior legal right pursuant to Article 23 of the Patent Law. Regarding the standing of a requester based on this specific ground for invalidation, this Court analyzes as follows from the perspectives of the essence of the regulated object, legislative purpose, and effect on legal order:

First, the essence of the regulated object. When a requester for invalidation files a request under Article 45 of the Patent Law, the grounds for invalidation asserted may, according to the relevant provisions of the Patent Law on the conditions for granting patents, be roughly divided into two categories: First, grounds for invalidation concerning substantive conditions for patent grant, such as patentability, novelty, inventiveness, utility, full disclosure, and support for claims by the description; second, grounds for invalidation concerning a conflict between the design patent right and another person's prior legal right. Because the essential attributes of different types of invalidation grounds differ, when the provisions of Article 45 of the Patent Law on the scope of persons who may file a request are applied to the above different types of invalidation grounds, the standing of the requester is closely related to the essential attributes of the invalidation grounds. After a patent application is granted, the patentee obtains an exclusive right to exploit the patent within a certain period. To ensure that the granted patent deserves such protection, the patent must truly meet the substantive conditions for patents, such as novelty, inventiveness, and utility, so that the protection granted matches its contribution. Any grant of a patent application that does not meet the substantive conditions for patents will improperly restrict the freedom of the public to use and innovate. To this end, the Patent Law establishes the invalidation system, aiming to discover and eliminate improperly granted patents with the help of the public, thereby maintaining a public space conducive to innovation. At the same time, for the public, they also have the ability and opportunity to obtain evidence concerning the substantive conditions for patent grant, such as patentability, novelty, inventiveness, utility, full disclosure, and support for claims by the description, and no practical obstacle exists. Therefore, the first category of invalidation grounds concerning substantive conditions for patent grant constitutes absolute grounds for patent invalidation, which may be asserted by anyone. For design patents, invalidation grounds concerning novelty and distinctiveness also constitute absolute grounds that may be asserted by anyone. Unlike the first category of invalidation grounds, the second category of invalidation grounds concerning a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right has its own special attributes. If a design patent right conflicts with another person's prior legal right, it directly affects only the prior legal rights and interests, without involving the public interest. At the same time, at the practical operational level, evidence proving that a design patent right conflicts with another person's prior legal right is usually only available to the right holder or interested party of the prior right, and others may find it difficult to obtain. Therefore, the invalidation ground concerning a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right is a relative ground for invalidation, which can generally only be asserted by the right holder or interested party of the prior right. The standing of a requester asserting this invalidation ground is naturally limited by the essential attributes of relative invalidation grounds.

Second, the legislative purpose of the provision on conflict of rights in Article 23 of the Patent Law. The provision that "a design patent right granted shall not conflict with another person's prior legal right" was added during the second amendment of the Patent Law, aiming to solve the problem of design patent applicants, without authorization, applying for design patents by combining objects to which others hold rights with their own products, thereby providing a legal basis for prior right holders to request the invalidation of the corresponding design patent. Therefore, the legislative purpose of this provision itself is to protect prior rights. Based on this legislative purpose, naturally, the right holder or interested party should assert this invalidation claim. Article 65, paragraph 3, of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (revised in 2001, hereinafter referred to as the Implementing Regulations), which complements the Patent Law, provides: "If a request for invalidation of a design patent is filed on the ground that the design patent conflicts with another person's prior legal right, but no effective decision or judgment proving the conflict of rights is submitted, the Patent Reexamination Board shall not accept it." The above provision of the Implementing Regulations specifies the acceptance conditions for an invalidation request based on conflict of rights from the perspective of evidentiary requirements, effectively restricting the standing of a requester for invalidation based on conflict of rights at the operational level, i.e., implementing the above legislative purpose at the practical level.

Finally, the effect on legal order. If anyone could assert the invalidation ground of a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right, it may produce undesirable effects on legal order. Allowing anyone to file an invalidation request on the ground that a design patent right conflicts with another person's prior legal right would inevitably lead to situations contrary to the will of the prior right holder. It should also be noted that the essence of a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right lies in the fact that the exploitation of the design patent right will infringe the prior right of another person. This conflict may be resolved if the design patentee obtains a license or consent from the prior right holder. Therefore, if a person other than the prior right holder or interested party initiates the invalidation procedure, the subsequent administrative procedure and administrative litigation procedure may become invalid at any time due to the elimination of the conflict of rights, resulting in a waste of administrative and judicial resources. Conversely, if only the prior right holder and interested party are allowed to assert the invalidation ground of conflict of rights, the above undesirable effects can be avoided.

Based on the above reasons, when the provisions of Article 45 of the Patent Law on the scope of persons who may file a request are applied to the invalidation ground concerning a conflict between a design patent right and another person's prior legal right, the standing of the requester for invalidation is restricted due to the essence of the regulated object, legislative purpose, and effect on legal order. In principle, only the holder of the prior legal right and interested parties may assert such ground. The second instance judgment, although reasoning from the particularity of the protected object of design patent, with reasoning that may be somewhat inadequate, reached the correct conclusion, and this Court affirms it.

(II) Whether a requester who meets the standing requirements at the time of initiating the invalidation administrative procedure loses standing due to a subsequent change in the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit

Article 249, paragraph 1, of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "In the course of litigation, if the disputed civil rights and obligations are transferred, it does not affect the litigation subject qualification and litigation status of the parties. The legally effective judgments and rulings made by the people's court are binding on the transferee." This provision reflects the principle of party constancy in civil litigation, which also serves as a reference for administrative litigation. According to this principle and spirit, in administrative litigation proceedings, after a people's court accepts a related lawsuit, to ensure the stability of the proceedings and avoid uncertainty in the litigation, the standing of a party is not lost simply because the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit subsequently changes. Conversely, if the standing of a party were allowed to be lost due to a subsequent change in the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit, rendering the already conducted administrative litigation proceedings invalid, this would have a serious adverse impact on procedural stability and certainty of results, resulting in a waste of judicial resources. At the same time, after the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit changes, the interests of the new right holder can be safeguarded through procedural design. For example, the new right holder may apply to substitute for the original party in the litigation, and the people's court decides whether to permit it based on the specific circumstances of the case. If the court grants permission, the litigation acts already completed by the original party are binding on the new right holder. For the administrative procedure for patent invalidation, it is characterized by the participation of both parties and the Patent Reexamination Board acting in principle as a neutral adjudicator, making it a quasi-judicial proceeding. The principle of party constancy may also serve as a reference for such procedure. Otherwise, it may similarly lead to instability in the administrative procedure for patent invalidation and a waste of administrative resources. Therefore, for a requester who meets the standing requirements at the time of initiating the invalidation administrative procedure, even if the legal relationship concerning the subject matter of the lawsuit subsequently changes, the requester does not automatically lose standing. In this case, assuming that Staples Inc. was indeed the copyright holder or an interested party of the work in question at the time of filing the invalidation request, even if it subsequently transferred the copyright to a third party, it would not thereby lose its standing as a requester for invalidation based on conflict of rights. The second instance judgment, by finding that the copyright in the work in question asserted by Staples Inc. had been transferred, denied Staples Inc.'s standing to file the invalidation request on the ground that the design patent in question conflicts with its prior copyright. This was an error in the application of law and should be corrected.

(III) Whether the second instance judgment correctly found that Staples Inc. is not the copyright holder of the work in question or an interested party

In this case, the second instance judgment, based on the grounds that Evidence 4 and Evidence 5 submitted by Staples Inc. conflicted with each other; Evidence 4, Evidence 5, Evidence 8, and Evidence 13 proving the same fact contained clear contradictions; and that the email in Evidence 14 mentioned the same model number as the design patent in question, found that Staples Inc. was not the copyright holder or an interested party of the work in question. In this regard, this Court holds that:

First, regarding the general principles and methods of evidence examination and determination. Article 54 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning Evidence in Administrative Litigation provides: "The court shall conduct a review of each piece of evidence that has been subject to cross-examination at trial and evidence not requiring cross-examination, as well as a comprehensive review of all evidence, follow the professional ethics of judges, apply logical reasoning and everyday life experience, carry out a comprehensive, objective, and fair analysis and determination, ascertain the evidentiary relationship between the evidence and the facts of the case, exclude evidence lacking relevance, and accurately determine the facts of the case." In the administrative procedure for invalidation of the design patent in question, Staples Company submitted Evidence 1 through 18 to prove its ownership of a prior valid copyright in the work at issue. Based on a comprehensive determination of the relevant facts proved by Evidence 6 and Evidence 14, and in combination with Evidence 4, Evidence 5, Evidence 13, the testimony of relevant witnesses who appeared in court, and the affidavits in Evidence 1, Evidence 3, and Evidence 12, the Patent Reexamination Board determined that Staples Company was the copyright owner of the work in question. The judgment of the second instance, solely on the grounds that some evidence contained contradictions and conflicts, upheld the first instance court's acceptance and factual determination of the relevant evidence, which violates the principle of comprehensive evidence examination and determination.

Second, regarding the examination and determination of Evidence 14. The judgment of the second instance affirmed the first instance judgment's conclusion not to accept Evidence 14, on the ground that an email in that evidence showing a generation time of November 2, 2007 mentioned a machine model that did not appear until more than a year later, presenting an apparent contradiction. The implicit logical premise of this determination is that the machine model in question factually came into existence before the filing date of the design patent application in question, February 22, 2008. In fact, there is no evidence in this case that can prove this logical premise. The above determination of the second instance judgment regarding Evidence 14 is clearly erroneous and should be corrected.

Third, regarding the examination and determination of Evidence 6 and Evidence 14. The first instance judgment, on the ground that both Evidence 6 and Evidence 14 contained the statement "This notarial certificate only objectively records the process of the party operating the computer and printing web pages on site, and does not prove the source, authenticity, or any facts other than the above preservation of evidence acts," determined that the above notarial certificates could not independently and certainly prove the source and content authenticity of the emails displayed therein. When examining and determining the authenticity and probative force of electronically stored evidence such as emails fixed in the form of notarial certificates, the court should comprehensively consider factors including the process of producing the relevant notarial certificate, the formation process of the email, and the content of the email itself, and make a determination on its authenticity and probative force in light of other evidence in the case. After examining the evidence, if the court is convinced that the existing evidence can prove the existence of the fact to be proved with a high degree of probability, and the opposing party's challenges to the corresponding evidence or the counter-evidence provided is insufficient to substantially undermine the probative force of the relevant evidence or to prevent the probative force from meeting the standard of proof of preponderance of the evidence, then the existence of the fact to be proved should be determined. The first instance judgment, relying solely on the statements in the said notarial certificates regarding the objects of proof declared therein, excluded the independent probative force of the said notarial certificates, and did not conduct an examination and determination in light of the formation process and content of the emails or other evidence; this was unbalanced. At the same time, as discussed earlier, the second instance judgment's examination of the email content in Evidence 14 was manifestly erroneous. Under these circumstances, the examinations and determinations of Evidence 14 and Evidence 6 by the first and second instance judgments were somewhat improper, and this Court specifically notes this.

In summary, the second instance judgment denied Staples Company's standing as the petitioner for the invalidation request on the ground that the copyright in question had been transferred, which constitutes an error in the application of law; its examination and determination of the relevant evidence violated the rules of evidence and should be corrected. This case should, on the basis of correcting the above error in the application of law, comprehensively review all relevant evidence submitted by both Staples Company and Luo Shikai, and re-examine and determine whether the evidence on record is sufficient to prove that Staples Company is the copyright owner or an interested party of the work in question, and whether the decision under challenge is correct.

Staples Company's application for retrial falls within the circumstances provided in Article 91 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 92, paragraph 2, of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 74 and 77, paragraph 2, of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

1. Order the Beijing High People's Court to retry this case;

2. During the retrial period, stay the execution of the original judgment.
